entries.displacement: port handling and rail path availability at the western interface
entries.falsification: Show that observed end-to-end variability is dominated by border-processing time rather than by waiting at the crossing; or that berth idle time at the eastern ports is already low, meaning the wait is a capacity constraint that scheduling cannot relieve; or that consignments already depart within a narrow window and the perceived irregularity sits in the rail haul.
entries.priorityRationale: Proposed first because it is the cheapest test of the pilot's own hypothesis. The pilot names "assuming port expansion removes ferry/coordination constraints" as a critical methodological risk, which makes the coordination question logically prior to any capacity addition: if scheduling relieves the wait, a berth programme was answering the wrong constraint. It reaches two functional links, maritime_crossing and modal_transfer, and its displacement is expected to be smaller than its relief because it moves a constraint westward into segments that already carry scheduled traffic. Preconditions are contractual rather than capital, so feasibility can be assessed without a financing question. Against the evidence criterion it ranks poorly and deliberately so: nothing here is sourced yet.
entries.summary: Publish a shared ferry slot schedule across the Caspian crossing and align berth allocation at both shores, so that a booked crossing has a known departure window rather than an open wait.
